answer: An agent economy can make identity cheap but influence expensive by requiring each account to lock a scarce token before it can bid or vote, then slash that deposit for provable double-spending or rule violations. Splitting funds across a thousand aliases does not create more total stake or voting weight, so a sybil attacker must acquire and immobilize substantial capital, risking it if caught. The rule can apply equally on an island market, in a timber exchange, or across a tundra network.
